periods.activity_title: How Big Is a Lakh? Building Number Sense

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.1 p.2
textbook_items_in_class.description: Choose a number for y. How close to one lakh is the number of days in y years? Also: if a person ate 3 varieties of rice every day, would they taste all lakh varieties in a 100-year lifetime? Standalone ? prompts building intuition about lakh.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: According to the 2011 Census, Chintamani's population was about 75,000. How much less than one lakh is 75,000?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimated population of Chintamani in 2024 is 1,06,000. How much more than one lakh is 1,06,000?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3
homework.description: By how much did the population of Chintamani increase from 2011 to 2024?

time_bands.activity: Anchor the magnitude of one lakh with the Eshwarappa story from the chapter opening: India once had a lakh varieties of rice. Students estimate aloud — hairs on a head, seats in a stadium — and the teacher draws the place-value pattern box (3-digit → 4-digit → 5-digit → 6-digit boundary values) on the board, establishing 1,00,000 as the smallest 6-digit number and reading it as ‘One Lakh’.

Students work on Figure it Out, section 1.1 p.2 (“Choose a number for y. How close to one lakh is the number of days in y years?…”) in pairs, computing days and comparing with one lakh. Brief whole-class share of results, noting that one lakh is simultaneously large (more than a lifetime’s days) and small (far fewer than lakh rice varieties tasted at 3/day).

Introduce the Indian place-value system’s 3-2-2 comma pattern. Students read and write six-digit and seven-digit numbers in words, then attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3 (“Chintamani’s population was about 75,000. How much less than one lakh is 75,000?”) and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3 (“Estimated population of Chintamani in 2024 is 1,06,000. How much more than one lakh is 1,06,000?”).

Class discussion: students share their answers and reasoning for the Chintamani questions, verbalising place-value position of each digit. Teacher consolidates the rule for reading numbers beyond a lakh in the Indian system.

periods.teacher_notes: The place-value pattern box is the structural spine of this unit — stress that each step multiplies by 10 and that 1,00,000 is reached exactly at six digits. Watch for students who write the comma in the wrong position (e.g., 1,000,00 instead of 1,00,000); the 3-2-2 rule needs explicit rehearsal. For self-study, the worked intuition in the chapter’s opening prose about hairs on a head and stadium capacity can be re-read alongside the exercises.
materials: Squared or plain paper for place-value box

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Thoughtful Thousands (+1000 button): how many presses to show (a) 3,000 (b) 10,000 (c) 53,000 (d) 90,000 (e) 1 lakh (f) ? for 153 presses (g) how many thousands make one lakh?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Tedious Tens (+10 button): how many presses to show (a) 500 (b) 780 (c) 1000 (d) 3700 (e) 10,000 (f) 1 lakh (g) ? for 435 presses.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Handy Hundreds (+100 button): how many presses to show (a)–(h) given targets; (i) hundreds to make ten thousand; (j) hundreds to make one lakh; (k) evaluate Handy Hundreds’ claim about numbers Tedious Tens and Thoughtful Thousands cannot show.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk Q2, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?

time_bands.activity: Introduce the three calculator characters from section 1.2: Thoughtful Thousands (+1000), Tedious Tens (+10), Handy Hundreds (+100). Students predict which character would need the most presses to display the same target number and note their predictions.

Students work in small groups on Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.5 (“Thoughtful Thousands: how many presses to show 3,000; 10,000; 53,000…”) and Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.5 (“Tedious Tens: how many presses to show 500; 780; 1000…”), recording press counts and noticing which targets are reachable by each character.

Groups take up Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.5 (“Handy Hundreds: press counts and Handy Hundreds’ claim…”), paying special attention to part (k) — which numbers Tedious Tens and Thoughtful Thousands cannot reach but Handy Hundreds can. Groups share their reasoning about reachability.

Whole-class discussion of Math Talk Q2, section 1.2 p.7 (“Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?”). Students articulate that the minimum press count equals the digit-sum — the class constructs this generalisation in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The key reasoning prize in this unit is the generalisation that minimum presses equal the digit-sum of the number — students often arrive at it by pattern but may struggle to say why; draw out the idea that each button adds a fixed place-value unit, so the digit at each place tells exactly how many presses of that button are needed. Watch for students who sum across all three buttons for the same number but do not distinguish which button covers which place. Math Talk Q3, section 1.2 p.7 (“expressions for least button clicks also give Indian place value notation”) is a strong self-study extension for confident students.

periods.activity_title: Creative Chitti and Systematic Sippy: Efficient Representations

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.6
textbook_items_in_class.description: Creative Chitti: for each of 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813, write expressions for at least two different ways to obtain the number through button clicks.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: For 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813: find the expression giving the smallest number of button clicks.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: Systematic Sippy: find how to get (a) 5072 and (b) 8300 using as few button clicks as possible. Write the expression.

homework.description: Creative Chitti challenges: (a) make the largest and smallest 3-digit numbers using exactly 30 button presses; (b) make 997 with a different number of clicks than 25.

time_bands.activity: Recall the digit-sum generalisation from the prior exploration of the three calculator characters. Pose: “If the minimum is fixed, can a number still be made in more than one way?” Students predict yes or no and briefly justify to a partner.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.6 (“Creative Chitti: write at least two different expressions for 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813”), writing additive expressions using the three button values. Pairs compare their alternative representations and discuss which use more clicks.

Students take up Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.7 (“For 8300, 40629, 56354, 66666, 367813: find the expression giving the smallest number of button clicks”) and Figure it Out, section 1.2 p.7 (“Systematic Sippy: fewest clicks for 5072 and 8300”). They write the minimal expressions and compare with the Creative Chitti expressions found earlier, noting the difference in click counts.

Whole-class share: two or three students write their minimal expressions on the board. Teacher consolidates the connection between the minimal expression and the Indian place-value decomposition of the number, reinforcing that each digit position maps directly to one button type.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly mix button types within a single place — e.g., using 8 hundreds and 3 tens to represent the hundreds digit of 8300 — which gives a valid but non-minimal expression; use this as a productive contrast when discussing Systematic Sippy’s strategy. The link between minimal-click expression and Indian place-value notation is the conceptual pay-off of this section — ensure at least one student voices it before moving on.

periods.activity_title: Two Systems, One Number: Indian and International Names

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.3 p.8
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many zeros does a thousand lakh have? How many zeros does a hundred thousand have? Standalone ? prompts on zero-counting for large named numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Read six numbers (4050678, 48121620, 20022002, 246813579, 345000543, 1020304050) and write their number names in both the Indian and American systems.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write four numbers in Indian place value notation from word descriptions spanning crores, billions, and millions.

time_bands.activity: Build the Indian naming ladder on the board: lakh (1,00,000) → ten lakh → crore (1,00,00,000) → ten crore → arab (1,00,00,00,000), using the 3-2-2 comma pattern. Alongside, construct the International ladder: hundred thousand → million → billion using the 3-3-3 pattern. Students count zeros at each step and work on Figure it Out, section 1.3 p.8 (“How many zeros does a thousand lakh have? A hundred thousand?”).

Students study the side-by-side comparison table from section 1.3 and then tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.9 (“Read 4050678, 48121620, 20022002, 246813579, 345000543, 1020304050 and write their names in both systems”), working in pairs. Each pair writes both names for at least three numbers.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.9 (“Write four numbers in Indian place value notation from word descriptions spanning crores, billions, and millions”), converting between word forms and numerals. Partners check each other’s comma placement and digit count.

Quick whole-class check: teacher calls out a number name in one system; students write its numeral with correct commas and then read it in the other system. Addresses common errors with the transition from Indian to International grouping.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error is misplacing commas when switching systems — a student who knows 3-2-2 may inadvertently apply 3-3-3 to an Indian number or vice versa; insist on rewriting the number from scratch with the target system’s comma rule rather than moving commas. The zero-counting prompt in Figure it Out, section 1.3 p.8 is a quick self-check: a crore has 7 digits (6 zeros after 1), and this anchor number helps verify larger names.
materials: Section 1.3 comparison table (from textbook or copied to board)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.3 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare and write ‘<’, ‘>’ or ‘=’ for: (a) 30 thousand vs 3 lakhs; (b) 500 lakhs vs 5 million; (c) 800 thousand vs 8 million; (d) 640 crore vs 60 billion.

time_bands.activity: Pose a warm-up conversion challenge: “Which is greater — 50 lakhs or 5 million? How do you decide?” Students discuss in pairs. Establish the shared approach: convert both to a common numeral form, then compare digit counts or leading values.

Students work through Figure it Out Q3, section 1.3 p.9 (“Compare and write <, > or = for (a) 30 thousand vs 3 lakhs; (b) 500 lakhs vs 5 million; (c) 800 thousand vs 8 million; (d) 640 crore vs 60 billion”), writing out both numbers as numerals before inserting the symbol. Each student justifies their inequality in a short written sentence.

Groups share their reasoning for the trickier comparisons — especially (b) and (d) — on the board, converting 500 lakhs to 5,00,00,000 and 5 million to 50,00,000, and comparing 640 crore with 60 billion. The class evaluates whether each group’s conversion is correct.

Consolidation: students pose one original comparison problem of their own (a named number in one system vs. a named number in the other), swap with a partner, and solve. Two or three student-generated problems are shared with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 5 million with 50 lakhs rather than correctly equating it to 50,00,000 — the section’s comparison table is the reference anchor; encourage students to re-derive the conversion rather than memorise it. Comparison (d), 640 crore vs 60 billion, requires multi-step conversion and is where confident students reveal whether they have internalised both systems’ structures.

periods.activity_title: Nearest Neighbours: When to Round and Why

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.10
textbook_items_in_class.description: Think and share situations where it is appropriate to (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either rounding is okay, (d) exact numbers are needed.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write the five nearest neighbours (nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh, crore) for: (a) 3,87,69,957 and (b) 29,05,32,481.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 1.4 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: I have a number for which all five nearest neighbours are 5,00,00,000. What could the number be? How many such numbers are there?

time_bands.activity: Open with the two everyday contrasts from section 1.4: ordering sweets (round up so nobody is short) vs. estimating a bill (round to nearest hundred is fine). Students work on Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.10 (“Think and share situations where (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either, (d) exact numbers are needed”), generating two examples per category.

Introduce ‘nearest neighbour’ rounding at five scales: nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh, crore. Students construct the rounding rule inductively by placing sample numbers on a number-line strip and identifying which ‘neighbour’ is closer. They then apply the rule to Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.11 (“Write the five nearest neighbours for 3,87,69,957 and 29,05,32,481”).

Whole-class discussion of Math Talk, section 1.4 p.11 (“I have a number for which all five nearest neighbours are 5,00,00,000 — what could the number be? How many such numbers are there?”). Students reason backwards from the rounding conditions to identify the range of values satisfying all five constraints simultaneously.

Pairs share their reasoning about how many numbers satisfy the Math Talk condition. Teacher consolidates the logic: students must reason that the number lies in the intersection of five intervals, each centred at 5,00,00,000 at a different scale, and identify the tightest constraint as the binding one.

periods.teacher_notes: The Math Talk problem is the reasoning centrepiece — students who can identify the tightest rounding constraint (nearest thousand restricts the range most tightly) demonstrate genuine understanding of what rounding means structurally, not just procedurally. A common error is rounding 3,87,69,957 to the nearest lakh as 3,88,00,000 by looking only at the ten-thousands digit and forgetting the midpoint rule; build the habit of identifying which side of the midpoint the number falls on. For self-study, Figure it Out, section 1.4 p.11 Q1 (estimation with Roxie and Estu) extends the rounding reasoning to sums.
materials: Number-line strips (drawn on board or paper)

periods.activity_title: Estimation in Context and Multiplication Shortcuts

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.11
textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate 4,63,128 + 4,19,682: evaluate Roxie’s and Estu’s estimates; determine if sum exceeds 8,50,000; determine if sum exceeds 8,83,128; compute exact value.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 1.5 p.14
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the meaning of multiplication and division, explain why multiplying by 5 is the same as dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.14

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 1.4 p.11 (“Estimate 4,63,128 + 4,19,682: evaluate Roxie’s and Estu’s estimates; determine if sum exceeds 8,50,000; determine if sum exceeds 8,83,128; compute exact value”), applying nearest-lakh rounding to evaluate both estimates and then checking against the exact sum.

Transition to section 1.5. Present Roxie’s method (Example (Roxie’s method), section 1.5 p.13): 116 × 5 = (116 ÷ 2) × 10 = 58 × 10 = 580. Then present Estu’s method (Example (Estu’s method), section 1.5 p.14): 824 × 25 = (824 ÷ 4) × 100 = 206 × 100 = 20,600. Students try two further examples of their own choosing before the Math Talk.

Students write a justification for Math Talk, section 1.5 p.14 (“Using the meaning of multiplication and division, explain why multiplying by 5 is the same as dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10”), using the fact that 5 = 10 ÷ 2. Pairs share and refine their explanations.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 1.5 p.14 (“Find quick ways to calculate (a) 2 × 1768 × 50; (b) 72 × 125; (c) 125 × 40 × 8 × 25”), applying Roxie’s and Estu’s methods to multi-factor products. Students write the shortcut step explicitly before computing.

periods.teacher_notes: The pairing of estimation (section 1.4) and shortcut multiplication (section 1.5) in this unit works because both demand that students rewrite a computation in a more convenient form rather than proceeding mechanically; the shared theme is ‘strategic rewriting’. Watch for students who apply Roxie’s method blindly to odd numbers — 5 = 10 ÷ 2 gives a non-integer intermediate when the number is odd, and this is worth discussing as a prompt to check divisibility before choosing the method.

periods.activity_title: How Long Is the Product? Digit-Count Patterns and Proof

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.14
textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate four sets of pattern multiplications (11×11, 111×111 …; 66×61, 666×661 …; 3×5, 33×35 …; 101×101, 102×102 …) and extend each pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15
textbook_items_in_class.description: Observe the number of digits in factors and products: is there a connection? Evaluate Roxie’s claim that the product of two 2-digit numbers is always 3- or 4-digit. Is there a better way than exhaustive checking?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can multiplying a 3-digit number with another 3-digit number give a 4-digit number? Can multiplying a 4-digit number with a 2-digit number give a 5-digit number?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15
textbook_items_in_class.description: Extend the digit-product pattern table: fill in results for 5-digit × 5-digit, 8-digit × 3-digit, and 12-digit × 13-digit.

time_bands.activity: Students evaluate the four pattern sets in Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.14 (“11×11, 111×111…; 66×61, 666×661…; 3×5, 33×35…; 101×101, 102×102…”) and extend each sequence by two more terms, recording the digit count of each product alongside the factors.

Students construct a digit-count table from their results (factor digits vs. product digits) and tackle Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15 (“Observe digit counts: is there a connection? Evaluate Roxie’s claim about 2-digit products”), reasoning about whether the claim can be verified without checking all products — leading to the boundary-case argument: smallest 2-digit product = 10×10 = 100 (3 digits); largest = 99×99 = 9801 (4 digits).

Students work on Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15 (“Can a 3-digit × 3-digit give a 4-digit? Can a 4-digit × 2-digit give a 5-digit?”), applying boundary-case reasoning: test the smallest and largest cases to determine the minimum and maximum digit count of the product.

Students extend the pattern table by filling in Figure it Out, section 1.5 p.15 (“5-digit × 5-digit, 8-digit × 3-digit, 12-digit × 13-digit”). The class formulates the general rule: the product of two d-digit numbers is either (2d−1)-digit or 2d-digit, and tests it against a non-square case (8-digit × 3-digit).

periods.teacher_notes: The boundary-case method — test the smallest and largest inputs to bound the output — is the key reasoning tool here and should be named explicitly; students who try specific middle-value examples risk missing the logical structure. A common error is to count digits in the factors separately and add them, giving (d₁ + d₂) always, without recognising the ±1 uncertainty; the boundary-case argument is what pins down the exact range.
materials: Notebooks (with space for a digit-count table)

periods.activity_title: Fascinating Facts and Open Estimation Challenges

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.16
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fascinating Facts — compute products/quotients to uncover hidden facts: (a) 1250 × 380 = kīrtanas by Purandardasa; (b) 2100 × 70,000 = approximate Earth-Sun distance in km; (c) 6400 × 62,500 = Amazon river discharge litres/second; (d) 13,95,000 ÷ 150 = longest single-train journey km; (e) 10,50,00,000 ÷ 700 = blue whale weight kg; (f) 52,00,00,00,000 ÷ 130 = global plastic waste weight in tonnes. Read results in both naming systems.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.18
textbook_items_in_class.description: Could Mumbai’s entire population (1 crore 24 lakh) fit into 1 lakh buses (50 people each)? Could it fit into 5000 Titanic ships (2500 passengers each)?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 1.6 p.21
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many coins (1 mm thick) should be stacked to match the height of the Statue of Unity (180 m)?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 1.6 p.21
textbook_items_in_class.description: Grey-headed albatrosses cover 900–1000 km/day. One of the longest trips is 12,000 km. How many days to cross the Pacific Ocean approximately?

homework.description: If Roxie travels 100 km/day, can she reach the Moon (3,84,400 km) in 10 years? Find out if you can reach the Sun in a lifetime travelling 1000 km/day.

time_bands.activity: Students survey the Fascinating Facts page and predict which computation will give the largest result. Brief pair-share, then the class lists the six computations on the board.

Small groups each take two or three computations from Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.16 (“1250 × 380 = kīrtanas by Purandardasa; 2100 × 70,000 = Earth-Sun distance…”), applying shortcut strategies (Roxie’s and Estu’s methods where applicable) or standard algorithms. Each group reads their result in both the Indian and International naming systems.

Whole-class estimation challenge: Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.18 (“Could Mumbai’s population fit into 1 lakh buses at 50 per bus? Into 5000 Titanic ships?”). Students compute 50 × 1,00,000 and compare with 1,24,00,000, then repeat for ships, writing their conclusions in a full sentence using the Indian naming system.

Students work on Figure it Out Q11, section 1.6 p.21 (“Coins 1 mm thick stacked to 180 m height of Statue of Unity”) and Figure it Out Q12, section 1.6 p.21 (“Albatross trip: 12,000 km at 900–1000 km/day”), making and stating their assumptions explicitly before computing. Final share: one group presents a computation and reads the result in both naming systems.

periods.teacher_notes: Encourage students to state assumptions before computing — for the coin-stacking problem, they must convert 180 m to 1,80,000 mm; a missing unit conversion is the most common error. For the Fascinating Facts, the shortcut methods from section 1.5 (Roxie’s ×5, Estu’s ×25) surface naturally in computations like 6400 × 62,500 — prompt students to look for these opportunities rather than multiplying directly. The Moon/Sun travel problems (Figure it Out, section 1.6 p.19) assigned as homework consolidate both large-number arithmetic and contextual estimation in a single extended calculation.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly reads the number 3,45,678 in the Indian place-value system?

options.label: A
options.text: Thirty-four lakh five thousand six hundred and seventy-eight

options.label: B
options.text: Three hundred and forty-five thousand six hundred and seventy-eight

options.label: C
options.text: Three lakh forty-five thousand six hundred and seventy-eight

options.label: D
options.text: Three lakh four thousand five hundred and seventy-eight

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three lakh forty-five thousand six hundred and seventy-eight.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the Indian 3-2-2 comma rule: the leftmost group (3) names the lakh's place, the next group (45) names thousands, and the final group (678) names hundreds, tens and units.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student grouped digits as 34 | 5678 (a 2-4 split) rather than 3 | 45 | 678, mis-identifying the lakh and thousands positions.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applied the International (3-3-3) grouping instead of the Indian (3-2-2) grouping, reading the number as three hundred and forty-five thousand.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student misread the thousands group as 4 (ignoring the 5 in tens-of-thousands), confusing the two-digit thousands pair with a single digit.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write the number with commas inserted by the 3-2-2 rule and name each group before choosing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write 3,45,678 in the International system and explain aloud why the name changes.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3
exercise.description: According to the 2011 Census, Chintamani's population was about 75,000. How much less than one lakh is 75,000?

items.prompt: How many zeros does the number one crore have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One crore is 1,00,00,000, which has 7 zeros.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build the Indian naming ladder: lakh = 1,00,000 (5 zeros); ten lakh = 10,00,000 (6 zeros); crore = 1,00,00,000 (7 zeros).

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student stopped at lakh (5 zeros), confusing one lakh with one crore.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student counted ten lakh (6 zeros), one step short of crore in the Indian ladder.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added one extra zero, possibly confusing crore with ten crore or with the International billion.

inclusivity.support: Refer back to the Indian naming ladder built in the textbook and count the zeros at each rung aloud.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write one crore in the International system and name the result.

exercise.description: How many zeros does a thousand lakh have? How many zeros does a hundred thousand have? Standalone ? prompts on zero-counting for large named numbers.

items.prompt: A calculator has three buttons: +1000, +100, and +10. Meera says the minimum number of button presses needed to display 4,305 is 12. Is she correct? Justify your answer by writing the expression that uses the fewest presses and explaining why no fewer presses are possible.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Meera is correct. The minimum is 4 presses of +1000 + 3 presses of +100 + 0 presses of +10 + 5 presses of... wait — 4,305 = 4×1000 + 3×100 + 0×10 + 5×... but there is no +1 button, so check: 4,305 cannot be reached by these three buttons alone since the units digit is 5 and no button adds units. Re-examining: 4,305 has a units digit of 5, which is not reachable by +1000, +100, or +10 (all add multiples of 10). Therefore 4,305 cannot be displayed by these buttons, and Meera is incorrect — no number of presses of these three buttons can produce a number with a non-zero units digit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each of the three buttons (+1000, +100, +10) adds a multiple of 10, so any reachable number must be a multiple of 10; since 4,305 has units digit 5, it is unreachable and Meera's claim is wrong.

inclusivity.support: Try pressing each button a few times and look at the units digit of the running total — talk through what you notice before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one digit of 4,305 to make the number reachable, then find the minimum presses for your new number and explain the connection to the digit-sum.

exercise.description: Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?

items.prompt: A number rounded to the nearest lakh gives 6,00,000. The same number rounded to the nearest ten lakh also gives 6,00,000. Explain what range of values the number could belong to, and state how many whole numbers in that range satisfy both conditions.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: For the number to round to 6,00,000 at the nearest lakh, it must lie in [5,50,001 … 6,49,999] (using round-half-up). For it also to round to 6,00,000 at the nearest ten lakh, it must lie in [5,50,001 … 6,49,999] — the nearest ten-lakh neighbours of 6,00,000 are 0 (too far) and 10,00,000; the midpoint is 5,00,000, so any number from 5,00,001 upward rounds up to 10,00,000 or down to 0 ... re-examine: ten-lakh neighbours of a number near 6,00,000 are 0 and 10,00,000; midpoint is 5,00,000. A number rounds to 10,00,000 if ≥ 5,00,000 (nearest ten-lakh). Wait — 6,00,000 is itself a multiple of ten lakh? No, 6,00,000 = 6 lakhs, not a multiple of ten lakh. Nearest ten-lakh values to 6,00,000 are 0 and 10,00,000; midpoint is 5,00,000. Since 6,00,000 > 5,00,000 it rounds to 10,00,000, not 6,00,000. Therefore no number can simultaneously round to 6,00,000 at the nearest ten lakh, because 6,00,000 is not a multiple of ten lakh. The student should recognise and state this impossibility.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply nearest-neighbour rounding at both scales: 6,00,000 is not a multiple of ten lakh, so no number rounds to 6,00,000 at the nearest ten lakh, making both conditions simultaneously impossible.

inclusivity.support: List the multiples of ten lakh near 6,00,000 (i.e., 0 and 10,00,000) and mark 6,00,000 on a number line between them to see which multiple it is closer to.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the target rounded value to one that is possible at both scales and state exactly how many whole numbers satisfy both conditions for your new target.

exercise.description: I have a number for which all five nearest neighbours are 5,00,00,000. What could the number be? How many such numbers are there?

items.prompt: Roxie claims: 'The product of any two 3-digit numbers is always either a 5-digit or a 6-digit number.' Justify this claim using boundary-case reasoning. You do not need to check all products — instead, identify the smallest and largest possible products and use them to prove the claim.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The smallest 3-digit number is 100 and the largest is 999. Smallest product: 100 × 100 = 10,000, which is a 5-digit number. Largest product: 999 × 999 = 998,001, which is a 6-digit number. Every other product of two 3-digit numbers lies between 10,000 and 998,001, so it is either 5-digit or 6-digit. This proves Roxie's claim without checking all products.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test the boundary cases (100×100 = 10,000 and 999×999 = 998,001) to establish that every product of two 3-digit numbers lies between a 5-digit and a 6-digit number.

inclusivity.support: Start by computing 100 × 100 and 999 × 999, count their digits, and then argue that all products in between must also have either 5 or 6 digits.
inclusivity.challenge: Extend the argument: for a d-digit number multiplied by another d-digit number, prove that the product is always either (2d-1)-digit or 2d-digit using the same boundary method.

exercise.description: Observe the number of digits in factors and products: is there a connection? Evaluate Roxie's claim that the product of two 2-digit numbers is always 3- or 4-digit. Is there a better way than exhaustive checking?

items.prompt: A calculator has only three buttons: +1000, +100, and +10. Write an expression (showing all button presses) to display the number 72,450 using the fewest possible button presses. How many presses does your expression use in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 72,450 = 72 × 1000 + 4 × 100 + 5 × 10. Expression: 72 presses of +1000, 4 presses of +100, 5 presses of +10. Total presses = 72 + 4 + 5 = 81.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the number in Indian place-value decomposition; each digit directly gives the count of presses for its corresponding button, and the digit-sum equals the minimum total.

inclusivity.support: Write 72,450 with commas (72,450) and identify the digit in each place — thousands, hundreds, tens — before deciding how many times to press each button.
inclusivity.challenge: Write a second valid expression for 72,450 that uses more than 81 presses and explain clearly which digit's contribution you have 'traded' into smaller units.

items.prompt: Insert the correct symbol (<, >, or =) between each pair and show your working by writing both numbers as numerals. (a) 45 lakhs __ 4 million   (b) 3 crore __ 30 million

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 45 lakhs = 45,00,000. 4 million = 40,00,000. Since 45,00,000 > 40,00,000, the answer is 45 lakhs > 4 million. (b) 3 crore = 3,00,00,000. 30 million = 3,00,00,000. Since they are equal, the answer is 3 crore = 30 million.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert each named number to its numeral using the Indian system (lakh = 1,00,000; crore = 1,00,00,000) and the International system (million = 10,00,000), then compare digit-by-digit.

inclusivity.support: Use the side-by-side table from section 1.3 to look up how many zeros each named unit has before writing the numerals.
inclusivity.challenge: Write a third comparison of your own — one number in the Indian system and one in the International system — where the two numbers are equal, and verify it.

exercise.description: Compare and write '<', '>' or '=' for: (a) 30 thousand vs 3 lakhs; (b) 500 lakhs vs 5 million; (c) 800 thousand vs 8 million; (d) 640 crore vs 60 billion.

items.prompt: Two cities had populations of 8,47,329 and 6,93,812 in a recent census. Priya estimates the total population by rounding each city's population to the nearest lakh before adding. Rajan rounds each to the nearest ten thousand before adding. (a) Find Priya's estimate. (b) Find Rajan's estimate. (c) Find the exact total. (d) Whose estimate is closer to the exact total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 8,47,329 rounds to 8,00,000 (nearest lakh); 6,93,812 rounds to 7,00,000 (nearest lakh). Priya's estimate: 8,00,000 + 7,00,000 = 15,00,000. (b) 8,47,329 rounds to 8,50,000 (nearest ten thousand); 6,93,812 rounds to 6,90,000 (nearest ten thousand). Rajan's estimate: 8,50,000 + 6,90,000 = 15,40,000. (c) Exact total: 8,47,329 + 6,93,812 = 15,41,141. (d) Rajan's estimate (15,40,000) is closer; it differs from the exact total by 1,141, while Priya's estimate (15,00,000) differs by 41,141.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each population to the specified scale using the nearest-neighbour midpoint rule, add the rounded values, then compare the absolute difference from the exact sum.

inclusivity.support: Use a number line to locate each population between its two nearest lakh (or ten-thousand) neighbours before deciding which is closer.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a rounding scale (nearest thousand, ten thousand, or lakh) that gives the closest estimate to the exact total and explain why that scale works best here.

items.prompt: A school library receives a donation of books. The librarian says: 'If we stack all 1,80,000 books one on top of another, each book being 2 cm thick, the stack would be taller than the Qutb Minar (72 m).' Is the librarian correct? Show your calculation and state the height of the stack in metres. Read your answer in the Indian naming system.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Height of stack = 1,80,000 × 2 cm = 3,60,000 cm. Convert to metres: 3,60,000 ÷ 100 = 3,600 m. The Qutb Minar is 72 m. Since 3,600 m > 72 m, the librarian is correct. In the Indian naming system, 3,600 m is read as three thousand six hundred metres.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of books by the thickness per book to get total height in cm, then divide by 100 to convert to metres, and compare with 72 m.

inclusivity.support: First find the total thickness in centimetres, then use the fact that 100 cm = 1 m to convert before comparing.
inclusivity.challenge: Find how many books would be needed for the stack to reach exactly 1 km, and read that number of books in both the Indian and International naming systems.

exercise.description: Fascinating Facts — compute products/quotients to uncover hidden facts: (a) 1250 × 380 = kīrtanas by Purandaradāsa; (b) 2100 × 70,000 = approximate Earth-Sun distance in km; (c) 6400 × 62,500 = Amazon river discharge litres/second; (d) 13,95,000 ÷ 150 = longest single-train journey km; (e) 10,50,00,000 ÷ 700 = blue whale weight kg; (f) 52,00,00,00,000 ÷ 130 = global plastic waste weight in tonnes.
